lines: Sit with that word for a second. Synchronised sounds like a solved problem, a box you check once and move past.
But both nodes can honestly report synchronisation and still disagree by more than the gap between two real writes.
So the question worth holding onto is what synchronised actually bounds, and what it quietly leaves unbounded.
Before you pick, notice what each answer is actually claiming about how the store decides.
One answer blames a particular clock's speed. The other blames nothing about speed at all, only about real time.
Ask yourself which of those two things a timestamp comparison can even tell apart.
answer: The later write, always, however fast or slow either clock happens to run.
A faster clock does not lose. It wins, by stamping an earlier real event with a larger number than a correct clock gives a later one.
Last-write-wins keeps the larger number, so the genuinely later write is the one thrown away.

lines: Resist the instinct that a correction happens once and the clock is simply fixed from then on.
An oscillator drifts continuously, so the correction has to run continuously too, against a target that never stops moving.
And that correction's own accuracy depends on something the protocol has no way to verify from inside itself: whether the path there and back took equally long.
Don't file this under a one-second rounding error. Spread over a full day, it is nothing like one.
Two clocks, each behaving exactly as its own design intends, compute different values for the same instant for that entire day.
Notice that neither clock is malfunctioning. Correctness and agreement turned out to be two separate things.
Keep these two clocks apart in your head, because collapsing them is where this goes wrong.
One answers how long something took. The other answers when something happened, and only on the machine that read it.
Neither was ever built to answer which of two events, on two different machines, happened first. A paused process defeats both anyway.
Here's the reframing worth keeping. A bounded clock is not more accurate than a point reading.
It is honest about how inaccurate it might be, and that is the strictly more useful property for a protocol to lean on.
A lease works the same way: it only survives if it outlasts the worst skew the clocks could ever disagree by, not the skew they usually show.
Watch what changes when the only thing you alter is which clock reads the result.
The identical skewed pair becomes a confident wrong answer under one reading, and an honest admission of doubt under the other.
Neither reading added information. One of them just stopped pretending to have it.
Carry forward the shape of this, not just the vocabulary.
A crystal drifts continuously, and the correction for it carries its own error bar, not a clean fix.
One extra second, split between two equally valid rules, cost a whole day of mutual disagreement, not a passing instant.
No clock type orders events across machines, and a bounded clock's real gift is admitting what it does not know instead of guessing.
Before you answer, ask what typical actually measures, as opposed to what a lease actually has to survive.
A month of real numbers tells you what usually happens. It tells you nothing about the one day that will not be usual.
answer: No. A lease is only safe if it outlasts the worst skew the two clocks could ever disagree by during its own length.
A single bad day, a delayed correction, a temperature swing, is exactly the case a typical number was computed to ignore.
And it is exactly the case the lease has to survive.
